claim: Active targeting and specific drug delivery to parenchymal liver cells is a promising strategy to treat various liver disorders.
source: Active targeting and specific drug delivery to parenchymal liver cells is a promising strategy to treat various liver disorders.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about targeted drug delivery approaches.

claim: Synthetic lipid-based nanoparticles were modified with targeting peptides derived from the hepatitis B virus large envelope protein (HBVpreS).
source: Here, we modified synthetic lipid-based nanoparticles with targeting peptides derived from the hepatitis B virus large envelope protein (HBVpreS) to specifically target the sodium-taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP; SLC10A1) on the sinusoidal membrane of hepatocytes.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study, which is supported by the methods and data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The targeting peptides specifically target the sodium-taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP; SLC10A1) on the sinusoidal membrane of hepatocytes.
source: Here, we modified synthetic lipid-based nanoparticles with targeting peptides derived from the hepatitis B virus large envelope protein (HBVpreS) to specifically target the sodium-taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP; SLC10A1) on the sinusoidal membrane of hepatocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the in vitro and in vivo experimental data showing NTCP-specific binding and uptake.

claim: Physicochemical properties of targeted nanoparticles were optimized.
source: Physicochemical properties of targeted nanoparticles were optimized and NTCP-specific, ligand-dependent binding and internalization was confirmed in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by the characterization data presented in Table 1 and related figures showing size, PDI, and zeta potential measurements.

claim: NTCP-specific, ligand-dependent binding and internalization was confirmed in vitro.
source: Physicochemical properties of targeted nanoparticles were optimized and NTCP-specific, ligand-dependent binding and internalization was confirmed in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and confocal microscopy data showing uptake in NTCP-expressing cells (Figure 1C, D).

claim: The pharmacokinetics and targeting capacity of selected lead formulations was investigated in vivo using the zebrafish screening model.
source: The pharmacokinetics and targeting capacity of selected lead formulations was investigated in vivo using the emerging zebrafish screening model.
evidence: This is supported by the zebrafish experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Liposomal nanoparticles modified with 0.25 mol% of Myr-HBVpreS2-31 showed an optimal balance between systemic circulation, avoidance of blood clearance, and targeting capacity.
source: Liposomal nanoparticles modified with 0.25 mol% of a short myristoylated HBV derived peptide, that is Myr-HBVpreS2-31, showed an optimal balance between systemic circulation, avoidance of blood clearance, and targeting capacity.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the zebrafish and mouse biodistribution data comparing different ligand densities (Figures 3, 4, 5).

claim: Pronounced liver enrichment was confirmed in mice by 111In gamma scintigraphy.
source: Pronounced liver enrichment, active NTCP-mediated targeting of hepatocytes and efficient cellular internalization were confirmed in mice by 111In gamma scintigraphy and fluorescence microscopy demonstrating the potential use of our hepatotropic, ligand-modified nanoparticles.
evidence: This is supported by the biodistribution data and gamma scintigraphy images in Figure 5 and supplements.

claim: Active NTCP-mediated targeting of hepatocytes was confirmed in mice by fluorescence microscopy.
source: Pronounced liver enrichment, active NTCP-mediated targeting of hepatocytes and efficient cellular internalization were confirmed in mice by 111In gamma scintigraphy and fluorescence microscopy demonstrating the potential use of our hepatotropic, ligand-modified nanoparticles.
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence and immunohistochemistry data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Efficient cellular internalization was confirmed in mice by fluorescence microscopy.
source: Pronounced liver enrichment, active NTCP-mediated targeting of hepatocytes and efficient cellular internalization were confirmed in mice by 111In gamma scintigraphy and fluorescence microscopy demonstrating the potential use of our hepatotropic, ligand-modified nanoparticles.
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy data showing intracellular localization of nanoparticles in Figure 6.

claim: Previously, hepatocyte targeted nanoparticles have been developed exploiting endogenous and exogenous targeting ligand-based mechanisms using glycan, protein or antibody modifications of the nanoparticle surface.
source: Previously, hepatocyte targeted nanoparticles have been developed exploiting endogenous and exogenous targeting ligand-based mechanisms using glycan, protein or antibody modifications of the nanoparticle surface (Akinc et al., 2010; Akinc et al., 2009; Barrett et al., 2014; Detampel et al., 2014; Witzigmann et al., 2016a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most established systems for liver-specific drug delivery rely on targeting the hepatic asialoglycoprotein (ASGPR) or low density lipoprotein (LDLR) receptors.
source: Most established systems for liver-specific drug delivery rely on targeting the hepatic asialoglycoprotein (ASGPR) or low density lipoprotein (LDLR) receptors.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field of targeted drug delivery.

claim: Less than 10 virus particles have been shown to be sufficient to efficiently target hepatocytes of chimpanzees resulting in a pathogenic HBV infection.
source: Less than 10 virus particles have been shown to be sufficient to efficiently target hepatocytes of chimpanzees resulting in a pathogenic HBV infection (Asabe et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The reason for HBV's extraordinary liver tropism is a highly specific amino acid sequence in the large HBV envelope protein (i.e. HBVpreS1 domain), which is essential for target receptor recognition.
source: The reason for its extraordinary liver tropism is a highly specific amino acid sequence in the large HBV envelope protein (i.e. HBVpreS1 domain), which is essential for target receptor recognition (Meier et al., 2013; Schieck et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In 2012 the interaction of HBV with the human sodium-taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP/SLC10A1) was identified.
source: For decades, the specific target of HBV on the sinusoidal membrane of hepatocytes was unknown until in 2012 the interaction with the human sodium-taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP/SLC10A1) was identified (Yan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the seminal discovery paper.

claim: Urban and colleagues performed a fine mapping of the HBVpreS sequence to identify the amino acids responsible for efficient binding.
source: Subsequently, Urban and colleagues performed a fine mapping of the HBVpreS sequence to identify the amino acids responsible for efficient binding (Schulze et al., 2010; Ni et al., 2014; Schieck et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Myrcludex B was developed as the first HBV/HDV entry inhibitor and successfully introduced in clinics (currently phase II clinical trials).
source: As a result, the first HBV/HDV entry inhibitor, a myristoylated peptide named Myrcludex B, was developed and successfully introduced in clinics (currently phase II clinical trials) (Blank et al., 2016; Urban et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical trial publications.

claim: Myrcludex B binds with high affinity and specificity to human NTCP on the sinusoidal membrane of hepatocytes thereby blocking binding of virus particles to their target cells.
source: Myrcludex B binds with high affinity and specificity to human NTCP on the sinusoidal membrane of hepatocytes thereby blocking binding of virus particles to their target cells.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Myrcludex B's mechanism of action.

claim: Several groups have attempted to develop targeting strategies based on HBV envelope proteins, for example recombinant HBV envelope protein particles (bio-nanocapsules) or HBV preS1-derived functionalized liposomes.
source: In recent years, several groups have therefore attempted to develop targeting strategies based on HBV envelope proteins, for example recombinant HBV envelope protein particles (bio-nanocapsules) or HBV preS1-derived functionalized liposomes (Liu et al., 2016; Somiya et al., 2016; Somiya et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previously developed nanoparticulate drug delivery systems had physicochemical properties (e.g. size, colloidal stability, and immunogenic potential), which were sub-optimal for efficient in vivo targeting of hepatocytes.
source: However, the nanoparticulate drug delivery systems developed had physicochemical properties (e.g. size, colloidal stability, and immunogenic potential), which were sub-optimal for efficient in vivo targeting of hepatocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' analysis of previous literature.

claim: Most developed formulations had sizes above the average diameter of hepatic fenestrations in healthy humans (i.e. 100 nm).
source: Most developed formulations had sizes above the average diameter of hepatic fenestrations in healthy humans (i.e. 100 nm) (Wisse et al., 2008) thereby limiting the passage through liver fenestrations and consequently the access to the space of Disse and the sinusoidal membrane of hepatocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and inference about the implications of particle size.

claim: The average diameter of hepatic fenestrations in healthy humans is 100 nm.
source: Most developed formulations had sizes above the average diameter of hepatic fenestrations in healthy humans (i.e. 100 nm) (Wisse et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The liver fenestrae diameter of rodents show high species and strain differences ranging from around 100 nm to 160 nm.
source: Notably, the liver fenestrae diameter of rodents show high species and strain differences ranging from around 100 nm to 160 nm, possibly explaining positive liver targeting of published formulations (Braet and Wisse, 2002; Steffan et al., 1987; Wisse et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A nanoparticle size above 100 nm triggers phagocytosis by cells of the reticuloendothelial system (i.e. hepatic Kupffer cells and spleen macrophages) resulting in rapid blood clearance.
source: In addition, a nanoparticle size above 100 nm triggers phagocytosis by cells of the reticuloendothelial system (i.e. hepatic Kupffer cells and spleen macrophages) resulting in rapid blood clearance (Kettiger et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The surface charge (i.e. ζ potential) should be slightly negative to prevent sequestration of particles in the lung or rapid clearance by cells expressing scavenger receptors.
source: The surface charge (i.e. ζ potential) should be slightly negative (Xiao et al., 2011) to prevent sequestration of particles in the lung (i.e. due to a positive charge) (Ishiwata et al., 2000) or rapid clearance by cells expressing scavenger receptors (i.e. due to an excessive negative charge) (Rothkopf et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: According to the classical Derjaguin-Landau-Verwey-Overbeek (DLVO) theory of colloids, a neutral charge has to be avoided to prevent particle agglomeration.
source: According to the classical Derjaguin-Landau-Verwey-Overbeek (DLVO) theory of colloids, a neutral charge has to be avoided to prevent particle agglomeration.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from colloid science.

claim: Steric stabilization by PEGylation mediates long circulating properties and prevents opsonization.
source: In addition to surface charge, steric stabilization by PEGylation mediates long circulating properties and prevents opsonization (Karmali and Simberg, 2011; Milla et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The lipid membrane composition used was based on a FDA and EMA approved multi-component lipid formulation based on Doxil.
source: For the lipid membrane composition, we used a FDA and EMA approved multi-component lipid formulation based on Doxil (i.e. liposomal formulation of doxorubicin) (Barenholz, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature about Doxil.

claim: Shan et al. reported huge discrepancies between in vitro systems and rodent experiments during the development of targeted nanomedicines.
source: Recently, Shan et al. reported huge discrepancies between in vitro systems and rodent experiments during the development of targeted nanomedicines (Shan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: All Myrcludex B derived (lipo)peptides were synthesized in high yields and purity by standard solid phase peptide synthesis using Fmoc-chemistry.
source: All Myrcludex B derived (lipo)peptides were synthesized in high yields and purity by standard solid phase peptide synthesis using Fmoc-chemistry (Schieck et al., 2013; Schieck et al., 2010; Müller et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the methods section and citations to previous work.

claim: Lipopeptides were N-terminally modified with the fatty acids myristic acid (saturated C14) or capric acid (saturated C10).
source: Lipopeptides were N-terminally modified with the fatty acids myristic acid (saturated C14) or capric acid (saturated C10), since our previous studies have shown that fatty acid modification is key for mediating interactions with target cells.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design and previous studies.

claim: Fatty acid modification is key for mediating interactions with target cells.
source: Lipopeptides were N-terminally modified with the fatty acids myristic acid (saturated C14) or capric acid (saturated C10), since our previous studies have shown that fatty acid modification is key for mediating interactions with target cells.
evidence: This is based on previous studies by the authors.

claim: Successful conjugation of Myrcludex B to lipid-based nanoparticles was demonstrated by fluorescence correlation spectroscopy using Myrcludex B-Atto488.
source: Successful conjugation of Myrcludex B to lipid-based nanoparticles was demonstrated by fluorescence correlation spectroscopy using Myrcludex B-Atto488.
evidence: This is supported by the FCS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The autocorrelation curve of nanoparticle conjugated peptides showed a significant shift to longer diffusion times as compared to the free peptide, with average diffusion times of τd = 1639 μs and τd = 192 μs, respectively.
source: The autocorrelation curve of nanoparticle conjugated peptides showed a significant shift to longer diffusion times as compared to the free peptide, with average diffusion times of τd = 1639 μs and τd = 192 μs, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the FCS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: All nanoparticles (Myrcludex B-derived peptide conjugated liposomes) had a spherical morphology with a small size around 90 nm, narrow size distribution (PDI <0.2), and a slightly negative zeta potential.
source: Light scattering and electron microscopy verified that all nanoparticles, that Myrcludex B-derived peptide conjugated liposomes (modified without or with C14 acyl moiety) had a spherical morphology with a small size around 90 nm, narrow size distribution (that is PDI <0.2), and a slightly negative zeta potential (Figure 1B, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the TEM images in Figure 1B and the characterization data in Table 1.

claim: Only a small increase in the hydrodynamic size of about 2 nm was observed after conjugation of Myrcludex B-derived peptides.
source: Only a small increase in the hydrodynamic size of about 2 nm was observed after conjugation of Myrcludex B-derived peptides (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the size measurements in Table 1.

claim: Nanoparticles modified with Cap-preS2-48 had an average diameter of 134.28 nm and a PDI of 0.24.
source: Exceptions were nanoparticles modified with Cap-preS2-48, which had an average diameter of 134.28 nm and a PDI of 0.24 (Figure 1B, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the characterization data in Table 1.

claim: The C10 acyl chain of Cap-preS2-48 interfered with liposome membrane stability.
source: It is tempting to speculate, that the C10 acyl chain of Cap-preS2-48 interfered with liposome membrane stability.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed instability of Cap-preS2-48 modified nanoparticles.

claim: Nanoparticles showed a high cytocompatibility up to the highest tested lipid concentration of 8 mM in all cell lines.
source: In all cell lines, nanoparticles showed a high cytocompatibility up to the highest tested lipid concentration of 8 mM, which is far beyond liposome blood concentrations achievable in a clinical setting (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 demonstrating no decrease of cell viability using the MTT assay) (Barpe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the MTT assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Myrcludex B-modified nanoparticles were rapidly internalized within 30 min into liver-derived HepG2 cell lines whereas no binding or cellular uptake was observed in non-hepatic HeLa cells.
source: In vitro uptake studies revealed that Myrcludex B-modified nanoparticles were rapidly internalized within 30 min into liver-derived HepG2 cell lines whereas no binding or cellular uptake was observed in non-hepatic HeLa cells (Figure 1C, representative confocal laser scanning microscopy images for Myr-preS2-48 modified nanoparticles).
evidence: This is supported by the confocal microscopy images in Figure 1C.

claim: Both the liposomal nanoparticle (DiI signal) and the encapsulated payload (carboxyfluorescein (CF) signal), were detected intracellularly.
source: Both the liposomal nanoparticle (DiI signal) and the encapsulated payload (carboxyfluorescein (CF) signal), were detected intracellularly.
evidence: This is supported by the confocal microscopy images showing both DiI and CF signals inside cells.

claim: CF was encapsulated into nanoparticles at a fluorescence self-quenching concentration (i.e. 60 mM).
source: Notably, CF was encapsulated into our nanoparticles at a fluorescence self-quenching concentration (i.e. 60 mM, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the fluorescence data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: CF fluorescence increases significantly after overcoming the Förster critical transfer distances, that is release of CF from nanoparticles into surrounding environment.
source: Thus, CF fluorescence increases significantly after overcoming the Förster critical transfer distances, that is release of CF from nanoparticles into surrounding environment (Chen and Knutson, 1988).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about fluorescence self-quenching and a citation.

claim: Specific uptake of nanoparticles with NTCP-binding component preS-peptide was enhanced with increasing SLC10A1 expression levels.
source: Specific uptake of nanoparticles with NTCP-binding component preS-peptide was enhanced with increasing SLC10A1 expression levels (Figure 1C,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4) demonstrating a high target specificity (i.e. HeLa WT <HepG2 SLC10A1).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry and microscopy data in Figures 1C, D and supplement 4.

claim: Nanoparticle modification with Myrcludex B-derived lipopeptides decreases the interaction with negatively charged cell membranes of SLC10A1-deficient cells (e.g. HeLa) due to a negative net charge of lipopeptides at physiological pH and thus increased electrostatic repulsion.
source: It is tempting to speculate that nanoparticle modification with Myrcludex B-derived lipopeptides decreases the interaction with negatively charged cell membranes of SLC10A1-deficient cells (e.g. HeLa) due to a negative net charge of lipopeptides at physiological pH and thus increased electrostatic repulsion.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed reduced uptake in HeLa cells.

claim: Overexpression of SLC10A1 in HuH7 cells resulted in a strong enrichment of cellular uptake ruling out an involvement of cell-line specific artifacts.
source: Uptake studies with a different liver-derived cell line (HuH7) comparing wild type and SLC10A1 overexpressing cells confirmed the SLC10A1 specific interaction. Overexpression of SLC10A1 again resulted in a strong enrichment of cellular uptake ruling out an involvement of cell-line specific artifacts (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Myr-preS2-31 modified nanoparticles successfully incorporated small molecular payloads as well as larger compounds (i.e. propidium iodide, doxorubicin, FITC-labeled peptide, DNA vector) to enhance their internalization into NTCP expressing cells.
source: In order to demonstrate the potential application of Myr-preS2-31 modified nanoparticles as drug delivery system, we successfully incorporated small molecular payloads as well as larger compounds into nanoparticles payloads (i.e. propidium iodide, doxorubicin, FITC-labeled peptide, DNA vector) to enhance their internalization into NTCP expressing cells (Figure 1—figure supplements 6, 7, 8 and 9).
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy and transfection data in Figure 1—figure supplements 6-9.

claim: Time-dependent uptake studies confirmed the rapid binding and internalization process of Myr-preS2-31 modified nanoparticles.
source: Indeed, time-dependent uptake studies confirmed the rapid binding and internalization process of Myr-preS2-31 modified nanoparticles (Figure 1—figure supplements 6, 7 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by the time-course microscopy data in Figure 1—figure supplements 6-8.

claim: Propidium iodide is a cell membrane impermeable drug.
source: Of note, propidium iodide is a cell membrane impermeable drug.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about propidium iodide properties.

claim: NTCP-targeted nanoparticles enabled internalization of propidium iodide into cells and successful release into cytosol indicated by nuclear counterstain.
source: Thus, NTCP-targeted nanoparticles enabled internalization into cells and successful release into cytosol indicated by nuclear counterstain (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy data showing nuclear staining in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: Modification of nanoparticles with Myr-preS2-31 significantly increases the transfection of NTCP expressing cells.
source: High content screening analysis demonstrated that modification of nanoparticles with Myr-preS2-31 significantly increases the transfection of NTCP expressing cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is supported by the high-content screening data in Figure 1—figure supplement 9.

claim: Fluorescently labeled Myrcludex B can be considered to be a suitable blocking agent since its binding to NTCP expressing HepG2 SLC10A1 cells results in a significant shift in fluorescence signal as compared to control cells.
source: Fluorescently labeled Myrcludex B can be considered to be a suitable blocking agent since its binding to NTCP expressing HepG2 SLC10A1 cells results in a significant shift in fluorescence signal as compared to control cells (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental data that is mentioned but not shown.

claim: Uptake inhibition of nanoparticles modified with Myr-preS2-31, Cap-preS2-48, and Myr-preS2-48 by free Myrcludex B was confirmed by flow cytometry.
source: Uptake inhibition of nanoparticles modified with Myr-preS2-31, Cap-preS2-48, and Myr-preS2-48 by free Myrcludex B-fluorescein was confirmed by flow cytometry (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data in Figure 2B.

claim: The uptake of Myr-preS2-48A modified nanoparticles was not significantly inhibited by free Myrcludex B, due to the non-specific amino acid sequence.
source: In contrast, the uptake of Myr-preS2-48A modified nanoparticles was not significantly inhibited by free Myrcludex B, due to the non-specific amino acid sequence (see difference in essential amino acid sequence highlighted in Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data in Figure 2B and the sequence information in Figure 1A.

claim: The uptake of NTCP targeted nanoparticles is an energy-dependent process.
source: By incubation of cells in presence of NaN3 or at low temperature (i.e. 4°C), we confirmed that the uptake of NTCP targeted nanoparticles is an energy-dependent process (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy data showing reduced uptake at 4°C in Figure 2A.

claim: Hepatotropism of nanoparticles is mediated by NTCP and the cellular uptake of the carrier is an active and energy-dependent process.
source: These results demonstrate that hepatotropism of nanoparticles is mediated by NTCP and that the cellular uptake of the carrier is an active and energy-dependent process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the competition and temperature-dependent uptake experiments.

claim: Only acyl modified peptides increased nanoparticle binding and internalization.
source: This set of experiments confirmed that the acyl modification of peptides on nanoparticles` surface is a crucial prerequisite for hepatocyte binding as reported recently for free peptides (Meier et al., 2013; Schieck et al., 2013). Only acyl modified peptides increased nanoparticle binding and internalization.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of peptide vs. lipopeptide modified nanoparticles and citations to previous work.

claim: Liposomes decorated with peptides conjugated to capric acid had a reduced colloidal stability.
source: Second, liposomes decorated with peptides conjugated to capric acid had a reduced colloidal stability. Their storage stability was limited due to particle aggregation.
evidence: This is based on observations of the Cap-preS2-48 modified nanoparticles.

claim: The size of Cap-preS2-48 modified nanoparticles (around 134 nm) exceeds the diameter of liver sinusoid fenestrations presumably limiting their access to the space of Disse.
source: Furthermore, their size of around 134 nm exceeds the diameter of liver sinusoid fenestrations presumably limiting their access to the space of Disse.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured size and known fenestrae dimensions.

claim: Myr-preS2-48A modified nanoparticles were excluded due to poor NTCP specificity as demonstrated by the lack of binding competition by free Myrcludex B.
source: Third, Myr-preS2-48A modified nanoparticles were excluded due to poor NTCP specificity as demonstrated by the lack of binding competition by free Myrcludex B.
evidence: This is supported by the competition experiment data in Figure 2B.

claim: The uptake of Myr-preS2-48A modified nanoparticles was independent of NTCP expression levels and even higher in HepG2 wild type cells.
source: In addition, the uptake of these nanoparticles was independent of NTCP expression levels and even higher in HepG2 wild type cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data in Figure 1D.

claim: Free Myr-preS2-31-K-Atto633 did not interact with PEGylated nanoparticles and thus did not trigger nanoparticle entry into HepG2 SLC10A1 cells.
source: Free Myr-preS2-31-K-Atto633 did not interact with PEGylated nanoparticles and thus did not trigger nanoparticle entry into HepG2 SLC10A1 cells.
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy data in Figure 2C showing no nanoparticle uptake when free peptide is mixed with PEG nanoparticles.

claim: Nanoparticles including their payload entered the target cell whereas the targeting ligand remained on the cell surface.
source: Interestingly, nanoparticles including their payload entered the target cell whereas the targeting ligand remained on the cell surface.
evidence: This is supported by the triple-labeling microscopy data in Figure 2C.

claim: Myrcludex B has a remarkably high affinity to the NTCP (KD of 67 nM).
source: Since Myrcludex B has a remarkably high affinity to the NTCP (KD of 67 nM) (Meier et al., 2013), it is tempting to speculate that the targeting ligand is retained by NTCP on the cell surface while the dissociated liposome payload is internalized and further processed by a yet unknown mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The targeting ligand is retained by NTCP on the cell surface while the dissociated liposome payload is internalized and further processed by a yet unknown mechanism.
source: Since Myrcludex B has a remarkably high affinity to the NTCP (KD of 67 nM) (Meier et al., 2013), it is tempting to speculate that the targeting ligand is retained by NTCP on the cell surface while the dissociated liposome payload is internalized and further processed by a yet unknown mechanism.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed separation of ligand and nanoparticle.

claim: Uptake experiments using pharmacological pathway inhibitors suggested a partially clathrin-dependent and caveolin-independent mechanism.
source: Uptake experiments using pharmacological pathway inhibitors suggested a partially clathrin-dependent and caveolin-independent mechanism, which differs from the process of phagocytosis and micropinocytosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data with pathway inhibitors in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Non-hepatic HeLa cells transduced with mouse NTCP (mNtcp; Slc10a1) or SLC10A1 can bind Myrcludex B-modified nanoparticles but binding is reduced as compared to binding in hepatic cell lines and no uptake is observed.
source: Intriguingly, additional factors besides NTCP binding seem to contribute to this process. Non-hepatic HeLa cells transduced with mouse NTCP (mNtcp; Slc10a1) or SLC10A1 can bind Myrcludex B-modified nanoparticles. However, binding is reduced as compared to binding in hepatic cell lines and no uptake is observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy and flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Additional hepatic cell dependent factors seem to play a role for efficient binding and internalization.
source: Thus, additional hepatic cell dependent factors seem to play a role for efficient binding and internalization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that NTCP expression alone is not sufficient for full uptake in non-hepatic cells.

claim: Verrier et al. reported recently that glypican five expression is an important co-factor for HBV entry.
source: Indeed, Verrier et al. reported recently that glypican five expression is an important co-factor for HBV entry (Verrier et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Binding of Myrcludex B alone is not influenced by glycosaminoglycans.
source: Notably, uptake experiments using psgA745 cells (CHO xylosyltransferase mutants) overexpressing NTCP showed that binding of Myrcludex B alone is not influenced by glycosaminoglycans (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Binding of nanoparticles could be partially inhibited in HepG2 WT cells using heparan sulfate suggesting an involvement of glycosaminoglycans in the binding and subsequent internalization process of nanoparticles for hepatic cells.
source: In sharp contrast, binding of nanoparticles could be partially inhibited in HepG2 WT cells using heparan sulfate suggesting an involvement of glycosaminoglycans in the binding and subsequent internalization process of nanoparticles for hepatic cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry and microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: With increasing targeting ligand concentration, a significant increase in cellular uptake was observed.
source: With increasing targeting ligand concentration, a significant increase in cellular uptake was observed (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry and microscopy data in Figure 2D and supplement 5.

claim: A threshold value of at least 0.25 mol% Myr-preS2-31 is necessary for efficient cell binding.
source: Notably, we identified a threshold value of at least 0.25 mol% for efficient cell binding by qualitative confocal imaging as well as quantitative flow cytometry experiments (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry and microscopy data in Figure 2D and supplement 5.

claim: A minimum of 80 functional maleimide moieties per nanoparticle is necessary for efficient cellular targeting after Myr-preS2-31 conjugation.
source: Thus, a minimum of 80 functional maleimide moieties per nanoparticle is necessary for efficient cellular targeting after Myr-preS2-31 conjugation.
evidence: This is based on stoichiometric calculations and the observed threshold of 0.25 mol%.

claim: The zebrafish is a valuable pre-clinical tool to assess the systemic circulation and blood clearance of nanoparticulate drug delivery systems in vivo.
source: Recently, we have reported that the zebrafish is a valuable pre-clinical tool to assess the systemic circulation and blood clearance of nanoparticulate drug delivery systems in vivo (Sieber et al., 2017; Campbell et al., 2018; Sieber et al., 2019b; Park, 2017; Yin et al., 2018; Sieber et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research by the authors and others.

claim: With increasing ligand density on the nanoparticle surface, the systemic circulation of nanoparticles decreased for both peptides.
source: With increasing ligand density on the nanoparticle surface, the systemic circulation of nanoparticles decreased for both peptides (Figure 3) indicating that ligand modification of nanoparticles interferes with the shielding properties of PEG.
evidence: This is supported by the zebrafish imaging data in Figure 3.

claim: Ligand modification of nanoparticles interferes with the shielding properties of PEG.
source: With increasing ligand density on the nanoparticle surface, the systemic circulation of nanoparticles decreased for both peptides (Figure 3) indicating that ligand modification of nanoparticles interferes with the shielding properties of PEG.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed decreased circulation with increased ligand density.

claim: Increased blood clearance was paralleled by accumulation in the posterior caudal vein region.
source: Increased blood clearance was thereby paralleled by accumulation in the posterior caudal vein region.
evidence: This is based on observations from the zebrafish imaging experiments.

claim: The observed binding pattern did not match a stabilin-2 scavenger receptor dependent nanoparticle clearance, which would be indicative for interactions with mammalian liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs).
source: The observed binding pattern did not match a stabilin-2 scavenger receptor dependent nanoparticle clearance, which would be indicative for interactions with mammalian liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) (Campbell et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with previous work and a citation.

claim: Sequestration by macrophages is responsible for the clearance mechanism corresponding to an accumulation in the spleen of rodents.
source: More likely a sequestration by macrophages is responsible for this clearance mechanism corresponding to an accumulation in the spleen of rodents (Sieber et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed clearance pattern and a citation.

claim: Nanoparticles modified with the shorter targeting peptide, Myr-preS2-31, showed increased systemic circulation as compared to Myr-preS2-48 modified nanoparticles at similar ligand densities.
source: Interestingly, nanoparticles modified with the shorter targeting peptide, that is Myr-preS2-31, showed increased systemic circulation (Figure 3B) as compared to Myr-preS2-48 modified nanoparticles (Figure 3A) at similar ligand densities.
evidence: This is supported by the zebrafish imaging data comparing the two peptides in Figure 3.

claim: Nanoparticles modified with more than 0.5 mol% Myr-preS2-31 were excluded from further evaluation due to their poor systemic circulation and high clearance rate.
source: However, nanoparticles modified with more than 0.5 mol% Myr-preS2-31 were as well excluded from further evaluation due to their poor systemic circulation and high clearance rate.
evidence: This is based on the zebrafish circulation data.

claim: Zebrafish xenotransplantation models are an emerging preclinical tool offering several practical advantages as compared to mouse xenografting models including prolific reproduction, facilitated xenotransplantation, and optical transparency enabling high throughput screening.
source: Despite anatomical differences with mammals, zebrafish xenotransplantation models are an emerging preclinical tool offering several practical advantages as compared to mouse xenografting models including prolific reproduction, facilitated xenotransplantation (no immune rejection due to limited adaptive immune response), and optical transparency enabling high throughput screening.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about zebrafish models and citations to previous work.

claim: A clear difference in targeting capacity dependent on SLC10A1 expression and ligand density was revealed in zebrafish xenotransplants.
source: Interestingly, a clear difference in targeting capacity dependent on SLC10A1 expression and ligand density was revealed.
evidence: This is supported by the zebrafish xenotransplant data in Figure 4.

claim: There was no significant difference in targeting capacity at different ligand densities for SLC10A1-deficient HEK293-GFP cells.
source: Whereas there was no significant difference in targeting capacity at different ligand densities for SLC10A1-deficient HEK293-GFP cells (Figure 4A), a significant increase in binding to HEK293-GFP cells was observed if SLC10A1 was overexpressed as the nanoparticles could bind specifically and be readily internalized (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the zebrafish xenotransplant data in Figure 4A.

claim: A significant increase in binding to HEK293-GFP cells was observed if SLC10A1 was overexpressed.
source: Whereas there was no significant difference in targeting capacity at different ligand densities for SLC10A1-deficient HEK293-GFP cells (Figure 4A), a significant increase in binding to HEK293-GFP cells was observed if SLC10A1 was overexpressed as the nanoparticles could bind specifically and be readily internalized (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the zebrafish xenotransplant data in Figure 4B.

claim: Nanoparticles modified with 0.25 mol% Myr-preS2-31 showed the highest targeting efficiency in zebrafish xenotransplants.
source: Most importantly, this was only valid for nanoparticles modified with 0.25 mol% Myr-preS2-31 (Figure 4, quantitative analysis).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative colocalization analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: Ligand density highly influences the balance between systemic circulation, systemic clearance rate and targeting efficiency of liposome-based nanoparticles.
source: This illustrates that ligand density highly influences the balance between systemic circulation, systemic clearance rate and targeting efficiency of our liposome-based nanoparticles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the zebrafish experiments comparing different ligand densities.

claim: Nanoparticles modified with ligand densities below 0.25 mol% show a favorable systemic circulation but have an insufficient targeting ability.
source: Nanoparticles modified with ligand densities below 0.25 mol% show a favorable systemic circulation but have an insufficient targeting ability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the zebrafish and in vitro experiments.

claim: Nanoparticles modified with higher Myr-preS2-31 targeting ligand densities (i.e. 0.5 mol%) have increased targeting ability in vitro but decreased systemic circulation and a high clearance rate under in vivo conditions.
source: In sharp contrast, nanoparticles modified with higher Myr-preS2-31 targeting ligand densities (i.e. 0.5 mol%) have increased targeting ability in vitro. However, decreased systemic circulation and a high clearance rate under in vivo conditions counteract the advantage of higher ligand densities.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: Nanoparticles modified with 0.25 mol% Myr-preS2-31 have the highest targeting efficiency due to an ideal balance between target affinity and long circulation time in vivo.
source: Nanoparticles modified with 0.25 mol% Myr-preS2-31 have the highest targeting efficiency due to an ideal balance between target affinity and long circulation time in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comprehensive in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: Nanoparticles are internalized by target cells whereas free Myrcludex B apparently binds with high affinity to target cells but is not internalized.
source: It should be noted that nanoparticles are internalized by target cells (Figure 4B) whereas free Myrcludex B apparently binds with high affinity to target cells but is not internalized (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the zebrafish imaging data in Figure 4B and supplement 1.

claim: This radiolabeling strategy has distinct advantages as compared to other labeling techniques or loading of 111In-oxine into nanoparticles.
source: This radiolabeling strategy has distinct advantages as compared to other labeling techniques or loading of 111In-oxine into nanoparticles (van der Geest et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on a citation to previous work describing the method.

claim: The radiolabeling method is robust, fast (within 45 min) and efficient with labeling efficiencies above 90%.
source: First, this radiolabeling method is robust, fast (within 45 min) and efficient with labeling efficiencies above 90%.
evidence: This is based on the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: DTPA-DSPE enables retention of 111In in serum for at least 48 h at 37°C (>98% label retention) demonstrating the high stability necessary for in vivo studies of nanoparticulate drug delivery systems.
source: Second, DTPA-DSPE enables retention of 111In in serum for at least 48 h at 37°C (>98% label retention) demonstrating the high stability necessary for in vivo studies of nanoparticulate drug delivery systems (van der Geest et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Free 111In is rapidly eliminated via kidneys and excreted in the urine.
source: Third, free 111In is rapidly eliminated via kidneys and excreted in the urine as shown previously (Harrington et al., 2000; Shih et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PEGylated nanoparticles showed the typical biodistribution of sterically stabilized nanoparticles with a strong signal in the blood.
source: PEGylated nanoparticles showed the typical biodistribution of sterically stabilized nanoparticles with a strong signal in the blood (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the biodistribution data in Figure 5A.

claim: Myr-preS2-31 conjugated liposomes demonstrated different biodistribution patterns depending on ligand density.
source: Myr-preS2-31 conjugated liposomes demonstrated different biodistribution patterns depending on ligand density (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the biodistribution data in Figure 5A.

claim: Modification of nanoparticles with 0.125 mol% Myr-preS2-31 did not alter the systemic circulation significantly.
source: Modification of nanoparticles with 0.125 mol% Myr-preS2-31 did not alter the systemic circulation significantly (i.e. high blood pool signal). Only a minor increase in liver accumulation was observed as compared to ligand-lacking PEGylated nanoparticles (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the biodistribution data in Figure 5A.

claim: Nanoparticles modified with 0.25 mol% Myr-preS2-31 significantly enriched binding to the liver.
source: Interestingly, nanoparticles modified with 0.25 mol% Myr-preS2-31 significantly enriched binding to the liver (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the biodistribution data in Figure 5A.

claim: Further increase in ligand density (0.5 mol%) resulted in an increase in spleen accumulation, that is enhanced clearance by cells of the reticuloendothelial system.
source: Further increase in ligand density (0.5 mol%) resulted in an increase in spleen accumulation, that is enhanced clearance by cells of the reticuloendothelial system (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the biodistribution data in Figure 5A.

claim: None of the nanoparticle formulation resulted in an elimination via kidneys demonstrating the high stability and retention of the DTPA-DSPE chelated 111In.
source: Of note, none of the nanoparticle formulation resulted in an elimination via kidneys demonstrating the high stability and retention of the DTPA-DSPE chelated 111In.
evidence: This is supported by the biodistribution data showing minimal kidney accumulation.

claim: Modification of nanoparticles with 0.25 mol% Myr-preS2-31 significantly increased the liver accumulation as confirmed by planar gamma scintigraphy imaging.
source: Modification of nanoparticles with 0.25 mol% Myr-preS2-31 significantly increased the liver accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by the planar imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplements 1-3.

claim: Further increase in Myr-preS2-31 modification (≥0.25 mol%) resulted in dominant location of radioactivity in the spleen.
source: Interestingly, further increase in Myr-preS2-31 modification (≥0.25 mol%) resulted in dominant location of radioactivity in an elongated structure in the far-left part of the abdomen under the liver, which was identified as the spleen (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the planar imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Elevated Myr-preS2-31 modification resulted in an exclusive spleen accumulation, that is enhanced clearance by cells of the reticuloendothelial system.
source: Indeed, elevated Myr-preS2-31 modification resulted in an exclusive spleen accumulation, that is enhanced clearance by cells of the reticuloendothelial system.
evidence: This is supported by the planar imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Elevated Myr-preS2-31 modification has negative impacts on liver accumulation in rats.
source: In order to exclude species specific effects, we also performed a planar gamma scintigraphy imaging of harvested organs from injected rats (Figure 5—figure supplement 4). Again, elevated Myr-preS2-31 modification has negative impacts on liver accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by the rat planar imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Nanoparticles modified with 0.25 mol% Myr-preS2-31 demonstrated a significant increase in the liver-to-kidney ratio.
source: Strikingly, nanoparticles modified with 0.25 mol% Myr-preS2-31 demonstrated a significant increase in the liver-to-kidney ratio confirming our conclusions from the zebrafish model, that 0.25 mol% Myr-preS2-31 is the optimal ligand density (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the ratio analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: PEGylated nanoparticles showed a weak fluorescent signal in the liver that was not associated with the sinusoidal membrane of hepatocytes but arose from the high hepatic blood supply.
source: PEGylated nanoparticles showed a weak fluorescent signal in the liver (Figure 5B). Importantly, these signals were not associated with the sinusoidal membrane of hepatocytes but arose from the high hepatic blood supply (Figure 5—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is supported by the fluorescence imaging data in Figure 5B and supplement 8.

claim: Modification of nanoparticles with 0.125 mol% Myr-preS2-31 did not result in significantly increased liver levels.
source: Modification of nanoparticles with 0.125 mol% Myr-preS2-31 did not result in significantly increased liver levels. A marginal binding of nanoparticles to hepatocyte membrane was visually observed (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the fluorescence and IHC imaging data in Figure 5B, C.

claim: Strong signals for nanoparticles modified with 0.25 mol% Myr-preS2-31 were observed on the basolateral membrane of parenchymal liver cells demonstrating the strong hepatotropism.
source: Importantly, strong signals for nanoparticles modified with 0.25 mol% Myr-preS2-31 were observed on the basolateral membrane of parenchymal liver cells (Figure 5B,C) demonstrating the strong hepatotropism of our nanoparticles.
evidence: This is supported by the fluorescence and IHC imaging data in Figure 5B, C.

claim: Nanoparticles modified with excessive Myr-preS2-31 densities (0.5 mol%) are rapidly cleared by liver resident macrophages, i.e. Kupffer cells.
source: We conclude that nanoparticles modified with excessive Myr-preS2-31 densities (0.5 mol%) are rapidly cleared by liver resident macrophages, i.e. Kupffer cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed diffuse hepatic staining pattern and spleen accumulation.

claim: Co-injection of Myrcludex B resulted in a clear decrease in liver enrichment by competitive inhibition of NTCP-binding.
source: Co-injection of Myrcludex B resulted in a clear decrease in liver enrichment by competitive inhibition of NTCP-binding as demonstrated by a change of signal.
evidence: This is supported by the planar imaging data in Figure 6B.

claim: Nanoparticles that were internalized into parenchymal liver cells did not co-localize with Slc10a1 fluorescent signals.
source: Interestingly, nanoparticles that were internalized into parenchymal liver cells did not co-localize with Slc10a1 fluorescent signals.
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 6C.

claim: Myr-preS2-31 still colocalized with Slc10a1 suggesting that the targeting ligand was separated from the nanoparticle during cellular internalization.
source: Myr-preS2-31 still colocalized with Slc10a1 suggesting that the targeting ligand was separated from the nanoparticle during cellular internalization as already observed in in vitro experiments.
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 6C and is consistent with in vitro observations.

claim: HBV binds to murine hepatocytes but cannot infect mice due to the lack of host cell dependency factors.
source: HBV binds to murine hepatocytes but cannot infect mice due to the lack of host cell dependency factors (Lempp et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Chimeric mice transplanted with primary human hepatocytes have been developed to study anti-HBV drugs.
source: Therefore, chimeric mice transplanted with primary human hepatocytes have been developed to study anti-HBV drugs (Petersen et al., 2008; Lütgehetmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: NTCP-targeted nanoparticles lack the species specificity of HBV and specifically bind to mouse hepatocytes in a Slc10a1-dependent manner and are subsequently internalized.
source: Importantly, our NTCP-targeted nanoparticles apparently lack this species specificity. In contrast to HBV, our hepatotropic nanoparticles specifically bind to mouse hepatocytes in a Slc10a1-dependent manner and are subsequently internalized.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mouse experiments showing uptake despite HBV's inability to infect mice.

claim: The combination of in vitro investigations, the zebrafish model and in vivo experiments in rodents offered a unique approach to optimize targeting ligand modified nanoparticles.
source: In conclusion, the combination of in vitro investigations, the zebrafish model and in vivo experiments in rodents offered a unique approach to optimize our targeting ligand modified nanoparticles.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about the overall experimental approach.

claim: The zebrafish model demonstrated to be an excellent tool to pre-screen various nanoparticle formulations, to assess the effect of Myrcludex B modifications on their pharmacokinetics and biodistribution, and thus increase the accuracy of predictions for experiments in rodents.
source: The zebrafish model demonstrated to be an excellent tool to pre-screen various nanoparticle formulations, to assess the effect of Myrcludex B modifications on their pharmacokinetics and biodistribution, and thus increase the accuracy of predictions for experiments in rodents.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the successful use of zebrafish to predict mouse results.

claim: The developed delivery systems can increase liver uptake levels, decrease accumulation in off-target tissues and at the same time avoid clearance by the reticuloendothelial system by mimicking HBV targeting properties.
source: The developed delivery systems can increase liver uptake levels, decrease accumulation in off-target tissues and at the same time avoid clearance by the reticuloendothelial system by mimicking HBV targeting properties.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about the performance of the optimized nanoparticles.

claim: Current liver targeting strategies such as ASGPR- or LDLR-targeted delivery systems suffer from certain drawbacks including complex synthesis of multivalent glycans or strong evidence that a majority of endocytosed gene carriers is recycled back to the cell exterior thereby reducing activity.
source: Despite the fact that current liver targeting strategies such as ASGPR- or LDLR-targeted delivery systems have already demonstrated improved drug and gene delivery in various preclinical models, these systems also suffer from certain drawbacks including complex synthesis of multivalent glycans or strong evidence that a majority of endocytosed gene carriers is recycled back to the cell exterior thereby reducing activity (Witzigmann et al., 2016a; Sahay et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Due to the availability of efficient peptide manufacturing protocols, the proposed NTCP targeted delivery platform is an alternative and promising approach which warrants further investigation.
source: Due to the availability of efficient peptide manufacturing protocols, the proposed NTCP targeted delivery platform is an alternative and promising approach which warrants further investigation.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the potential of the developed platform.
